questions.q: Where does the actual connection between a scoped application and an external Git repository happen?
options: At the application record level in Studio, linked to a specific repository URL
Inside an Update Set that must be preview-committed first
Only through a third-party browser extension, never inside the instance
At the user profile level, not the application level
questions.explain: The scoped application record in Studio is linked to a repository URL on a provider like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.

questions.q: What does connecting to a repository require before any code can move in either direction?
options: Configuring real credentials so the instance can authenticate as a user or service account with push and pull access
Nothing — any ServiceNow instance can push to any public repository with no setup
Deleting all existing Update Sets on the instance first
Converting the scoped application into a global application
questions.explain: A Git repository requires real authentication; the instance needs credentials proving it's allowed to read and write to that repository.

questions.q: What does a 'push' do once the connection to a Git repository is authenticated?
options: It sends changes made inside the ServiceNow instance out to the repository, recorded as a real commit
It brings changes from the repository back into the instance
It deletes the repository's commit history
It converts the application back into Update Sets
questions.explain: Push moves changes from the instance outward to the repository. Pull is the reverse direction.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat the connection credential as a real security consideration, not just a setup detail?
options: Because that credential effectively has write access to the application's entire codebase
Because credentials are only used once and then automatically deleted
Because the credential only grants read access and nothing else
Because Git repositories don't actually require any authentication
questions.explain: Write access to an entire application's code is significant access — the lesson says it should get the same care as any other production credential.

questions.q: What is the real practical shift this lesson describes once an application is connected to a Git repository?
options: The application can be committed, pushed, branched, and pulled using the same Git habits a development team already has
The application no longer has any component records inside the ServiceNow instance
Studio becomes unnecessary and is no longer used at all
The application can only be edited by ServiceNow support staff from then on
questions.explain: The connection doesn't teach a new skill from scratch — it lets the same Git workflow already used elsewhere apply directly to a ServiceNow application.
